title: Cholinergic modulation and other gates

The preceding subsections established the molecular machinery by which dopaminergic prediction errors write into corticostriatal synaptic weights through opponent, pathway-specific plasticity rules operating on eligibility traces. But dopamine is not the only neuromodulatory signal that determines whether a given corticostriatal synapse undergoes lasting change. As emphasized in the error-signal section, cholinergic interneurons (CINs) generate a dense, tonically active acetylcholine field within the striatum whose transient pauses and rebounds are time-locked to behaviorally salient events. This section now revisits the cholinergic system through the lens of plasticity proper, asking: how does acetylcholine gate, sculpt, and in some cases independently drive the synaptic changes that update the striatal policy?

A direct demonstration that cholinergic pauses are not merely correlated with but causally required for corticostriatal plasticity came from Zhang, Fisher, and colleagues, who independently manipulated CIN activity and midbrain dopamine neuron activity in two complementary in vivo paradigms. Their central finding was that long-term potentiation at corticostriatal synapses onto SPNs required the triple coincidence of three events: (i) a pause in CIN firing, (ii) phasic activation of dopamine neurons, and (iii) depolarization of the postsynaptic SPN 1. Neither phasic dopamine alone nor CIN pauses alone were sufficient; only their temporal overlap, combined with ongoing SPN depolarization, produced durable potentiation. This triple-coincidence requirement has important computational consequences. First, the CIN pause defines a temporal window for plasticity: because dopamine neurons fire phasically in response to many behavioral variables beyond reward prediction errors–including salience, novelty, and movement initiation–unrestricted dopamine-dependent plasticity would corrupt stored action values with irrelevant updates. By gating plasticity to epochs in which CIN firing is simultaneously suppressed, the system restricts synaptic modification to those dopaminergic events that co-occur with the particular constellation of thalamostriatal and cortical inputs that drive the CIN pause, thereby implementing a form of contextual credit assignment 1. Second, the requirement for SPN depolarization provides a spatial constraint: because volume-transmitted dopamine bathes a broad region of striatum, the depolarization criterion ensures that only those spines whose corticostriatal inputs are currently active—and whose parent SPN is therefore depolarized—are eligible for modification. In reinforcement-learning terms, the CIN pause supplies the "when to learn" gate, dopamine supplies the "how much and in what direction" teaching signal, and SPN depolarization supplies the "which synapses" specificity 1. A 2025 slice study examines cholinergic burst–pause responses (Figure) 46. The study tests the mechanism of the pause (Figure). The study manipulates dopamine receptors (Figure).

An important qualification of this picture has emerged from recent work using opto-tagged, positively identified CINs recorded alongside simultaneous dopamine measurements across striatal subregions during decision-making behavior. Duhne, Mohebi, and colleagues found that the classical expectation—CIN pauses temporally aligned with dopaminergic reward prediction errors—did not hold uniformly across the striatum 2. In dorsolateral striatum, a Go cue evoked a CIN burst-pause sequence followed by a brief dopamine pulse that was unrelated to RPE; in dorsomedial striatum, the same cue evoked a CIN pause that was curtailed by a movement-selective rebound; and in ventral striatum, a reward cue evoked RPE-scaled increases in both dopamine and CIN firing, without a consistent pause. These findings do not invalidate the triple-coincidence principle, but they critically constrain its scope: the simple model in which a uniform CIN pause and a uniform dopamine RPE converge everywhere in striatum to gate learning must be replaced by a regionally parameterized account in which the phase relationship between cholinergic and dopaminergic dynamics varies across striatal territories, implying that different subregions may implement different plasticity regimes under the same behavioral contingency 2. A 2025 study measures acetylcholine across mouse striatum (Figure). The study analyzes spatial and temporal variation (Figure).

This regional parameterization has been given a precise functional interpretation by Jang, Ward, Golden, and Constantinople, who simultaneously measured dopamine and acetylcholine release in the dorsomedial striatum of rats performing a decision-making task and found that dopamine served different computational roles depending on its phase relationship to cholinergic dynamics 3. When a dopamine transient slightly lagged a cholinergic dip at the time of an offer cue, it predicted behavioral updating on subsequent trials and was associated with trial-to-trial changes in dorsomedial striatal firing rates—hallmarks of dopamine-dependent plasticity. When a dopamine transient preceded a cholinergic dip, no comparable relationship to subsequent learning was detected. And when dopamine was coincident with cholinergic bursts rather than dips—as occurred at movement-related events—it predicted the vigor of upcoming contralateral orienting movements without evidence of lasting plasticity 3. The implication for synaptic learning is direct: local cholinergic timing can demix the multiplexed content of a single dopaminergic signal into at least two downstream modes—a plasticity-promoting mode gated by cholinergic pauses, and a transient performance/vigor mode coincident with cholinergic bursts. In reinforcement-learning terms, acetylcholine determines whether a given dopamine transient functions as a teaching signal that updates corticostriatal weights or as a transient gain signal that modulates the vigor of the currently selected action without modifying the underlying policy.

The molecular pathways through which tonic acetylcholine influences corticostriatal plasticity are multiple and partially opposing. At the postsynaptic level, tonic muscarinic M1 receptor activation on SPNs tends to enhance excitability and depolarization, but also inhibits CaV1.3-type L-type calcium channels, which are required for endocannabinoid-dependent long-term depression; the net effect of sustained M1 signaling is therefore to suppress the induction of eCB-LTD 4, 5. During a CIN pause, M1 receptor stimulation is transiently relieved, permitting calcium channel activation and eCB mobilization—one route by which the pause can be permissive for depression as well as for potentiation. At the level of direct-pathway SPNs, the Gi-coupled M4 muscarinic receptor plays a particularly important role: M4 is an abundant muscarinic subtype in the striatum and is preferentially expressed in dSPNs, where it is clustered near axospinous glutamatergic synapses 6. One study showed that endogenous cholinergic signaling through M4 receptors promotes long-term depression at dSPN corticostriatal synapses by suppressing regulator of G-protein signaling type 4 (RGS4) activity, and blocks D1 receptor-dependent LTP; boosting M4 signaling with a positive allosteric modulator was sufficient to block aberrant LTP in dSPNs in a mouse model of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia and enabled depotentiation of pathologically strengthened synapses 6. The M4 receptor on dSPNs thus acts as a cholinergic counterweight to D1-mediated potentiation: tonic acetylcholine, via M4, biases dSPN corticostriatal synapses toward depression and away from runaway potentiation, and the CIN pause transiently releases this brake, opening a window in which D1-dependent LTP can proceed 6, 7. On the presynaptic side, M2/M4 autoreceptors on cholinergic terminals and M2-like receptors on corticostriatal terminals add further complexity: blockade of presynaptic M2-like receptors enhances striatal LTP by relieving inhibition of glutamate release, and genetic deletion of M2/M4 receptors abolishes both LTD induction and synaptic depotentiation 8. The picture that emerges is of a cholinergic system that, through multiple receptor subtypes acting at pre- and postsynaptic sites, exerts a tonic bidirectional bias on the plasticity landscape: sustained acetylcholine promotes certain forms of depression (via M4 on dSPNs and eCB-related pathways) and suppresses others (via M1-mediated calcium channel inhibition), while the CIN pause transiently reconfigures this landscape to favor whichever form of plasticity is appropriate to the concurrent dopaminergic and depolarization signals. The molecular pathways through which tonic acetylcholine influences corticostriatal plasticity are multiple, distributed across pre- and postsynaptic sites, and in several cases partially opposing. At the postsynaptic level, tonic muscarinic M1 receptor activation on SPNs tends to enhance excitability and depolarization, increasing dendritic responsiveness to corticostriatal input via mechanisms that include KCNQ potassium-channel regulation and endocannabinoid-related signaling 9, 10, 11. At the same time, M1 signaling can oppose at least some forms of corticostriatal depression by inhibiting CaV1.3-type L-type calcium channels required for endocannabinoid-dependent LTD, so the net contribution of tonic M1 activation is not a simple push toward either potentiation or depression, but a state-dependent reshaping of which plasticity rules are available under current conditions 4, 5. Notably, the excitatory effect of M1 stimulation appears especially prominent in D2-expressing indirect-pathway SPNs, suggesting that tonic acetylcholine can differentially regulate pathway excitability even before dopaminergic teaching signals arrive 11. During a CIN pause, this tonic muscarinic drive is transiently relieved, permitting a rapid reconfiguration of the local plasticity landscape; in that interval, relief of M1-dependent constraints may facilitate calcium-channel activation and endocannabinoid mobilization, making the pause permissive for depression in some contexts and for potentiation in others, depending on the coincident dopaminergic and depolarizing state of the SPN 4, 5.

At the level of direct-pathway SPNs, the Gi-coupled M4 muscarinic receptor plays a particularly important role. M4 is an abundant striatal muscarinic subtype, densely co-expressed with D1 receptors on MSNs and especially important in D1-linked signaling regimes, where it acts as a functional antagonist of D1 receptor-mediated cAMP-dependent cascades 12, 13, 14, 15. Consistent with this, endogenous cholinergic signaling through M4 receptors has been shown to promote depression-like plasticity states at dSPN corticostriatal synapses, to suppress regulator of G-protein signaling type 4 (RGS4) activity, and to oppose D1-dependent LTP; boosting M4 signaling with a positive allosteric modulator can block aberrant potentiation and restore depotentiation of pathologically strengthened synapses in models of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia 6. M4 receptors on MSNs have also been implicated in prolonged suppression of dopamine release through a cannabinoid CB2-dependent mechanism, further reinforcing the idea that M4 provides a cholinergic counterweight to dopaminergic gain 16. Mechanistically, this signaling can itself be potentiated by calcium influx, because Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase IIα\alpha binds directly and selectively to M4 and strengthens M4 receptor signaling 17, 18.

On the presynaptic side, cholinergic control adds yet another layer of regulation. Striatal CINs express Gi-coupled M2 and M4 autoreceptors, whose activation suppresses cholinergic tone and, through a disynaptic mechanism, reduces nicotinic acetylcholine receptor-dependent dopamine transmission 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. This modulation is not merely inhibitory in a static sense: it also changes the frequency sensitivity of dopamine release, with M2 and M4 contributing in dorsal striatum and M4 appearing to dominate more strongly in ventral striatum/nucleus accumbens 23, 24. In parallel, stimulation of presynaptic M4 receptors on corticostriatal terminals depresses glutamatergic transmission itself 25, 26, 27. Consistent with this broader inhibitory role, M4 knockout increases psychostimulant-evoked extracellular dopamine efflux in nucleus accumbens, whereas M2 knockout does not produce the same ventral-striatal phenotype; conversely, M1 knockout elevates extracellular dopamine and exacerbates amphetamine-evoked dopamine efflux despite normal whole-tissue dopamine content 28, 29, 30, 31. The picture that emerges is therefore of a cholinergic system that exerts a tonic, multi-level, and state-dependent bias on the corticostriatal plasticity landscape: sustained acetylcholine can enhance SPN responsiveness through M1, oppose D1-driven potentiation through M4, suppress glutamate release through presynaptic M4 receptors, and regulate dopamine transmission through M2/M4-dependent control of CIN tone; the CIN pause then transiently releases selected components of this cholinergic constraint, opening a brief window in which the sign and magnitude of plasticity can be more strongly determined by coincident dopaminergic error signals and postsynaptic depolarization.

Beyond gating dopamine-dependent plasticity, cholinergic dynamics in some striatal territories appear to carry error-like information of their own that can drive plasticity independently or in opposition to dopamine. During Pavlovian learning and extinction, anterior dorsal striatal acetylcholine exhibited phase-specific prediction-error structure: positive and negative RPE-like signals were expressed in different temporal components of the acetylcholine waveform, and silencing local acetylcholine release impaired extinction while sparing initial acquisition 32. In reversal-learning paradigms, dorsal striatal acetylcholine elevations following unexpected non-reward were causally required for behavioral adaptation: optogenetic silencing of CINs selectively impaired the ability of mice to switch away from a previously rewarded choice 33. These findings converge with the opponent-plasticity data reviewed earlier to suggest that cholinergic circuitry is especially important for negative updating, extinction, and contingency revision–precisely the situations in which cached action values must be weakened rather than strengthened. A 2026 preprint links striatal acetylcholine dip–rebound dynamics to action–outcome learning and extinction (Figure) 45. The authors test the behavioral role of acetylcholine release (Figure).

A computational model by Kim and colleagues formalizes and extends these ideas, showing that cholinergic pauses can solve a structural credit-assignment problem that dopamine alone cannot 34. The model implements a biologically plausible three-factor learning rule requiring presynaptic activity, postsynaptic depolarization, and phasic dopamine, with plasticity gated by cholinergic pauses that temporally align with behaviorally relevant events. In environments with many competing stimuli and actions—where dopamine is broadcast globally and cannot by itself identify which stimulus–action channel was responsible for the outcome—the cholinergic pause restricts plasticity to the channel that was active around action execution, preventing catastrophic interference across channels. Without this cholinergic gate, learning degrades severely as the number of actions increases; with it, the system scales gracefully 34. This result resonates with earlier computational accounts in which TAN pauses regulate the effective learning rate by modulating SPN excitability and population-level uncertainty 35, and with models in which the CIN pause protects stored action values from decay during periods of non-reward by suppressing corticostriatal throughput 36.

The local neuromodulatory field in which corticostriatal plasticity is embedded is, however, becoming richer than the dopamine-acetylcholine dyad alone. Serotonin, supplied to the striatum predominantly by dorsal raphe projections, can itself induce a presynaptically mediated long-term depression of corticostriatal glutamate release via 5-HT1b receptors–a form of plasticity (5-HT-LTD) that is mutually occlusive with the canonical dopamine/endocannabinoid-dependent LTD, suggesting that the two forms of depression converge on overlapping, and possibly the same, populations of corticostriatal terminals 37. Importantly, CINs are now known to shape local striatal serotonin signaling more directly than previously appreciated: Matityahu, Hobel, and colleagues showed that synchronous activation of CINs triggers local serotonin release in the dorsal striatum via nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on serotonergic axons, thereby extending the spatial range of serotonergic signaling; this coupling is exaggerated in the hypercholinergic striatum of Sapap3-/- mice 38. Thus, CINs can influence corticostriatal plasticity not only through their direct muscarinic and nicotinic actions on dopamine terminals and SPNs, but also by modulating local serotonergic tone–potentially recruiting an additional serotonergic route to synaptic depression under appropriate circuit conditions.

Finally, the GABAergic interneuron network within the striatum contributes an additional layer of plasticity control that is only beginning to be characterized. Two interneuron subtypes deserve particular mention. Somatostatin-expressing (SOM) interneurons (also termed low-threshold spiking interneurons, LTSIs) are sparse but tonically active cells that preferentially target SPN distal dendrites and exert especially potent feedforward inhibition in dorsomedial striatum 39, 40. Rotariu and colleagues showed that selective manipulation of SOM interneurons disrupted the reorganization of dorsomedial striatal activity during early motor learning–the experience-dependent emergence of a sparse, high-activity SPN ensemble whose size correlates with task performance–whereas manipulation of parvalbumin (PV) interneurons in the same region had no effect 41. SOM-to-SPN inhibitory connections in dorsomedial striatum proved to be highly plastic: their synaptic strength was significantly enhanced after early training, suggesting that SOM interneurons actively sculpt the representational landscape through learning-dependent changes in their own synaptic output 41. SOM interneurons also locally gate dopamine release via GABA-B signaling on dopaminergic terminals, providing a mechanism by which this interneuron class can regulate both the excitability of SPN dendritic compartments and the magnitude of the teaching signal that reaches them 42. Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) fast-spiking interneurons, by contrast, exert especially strong control in DLS, target SPN somata and proximal dendrites, and exert their strongest influence on striatal output during the early phases of associative learning: optogenetic and chemogenetic suppression of PV cells impaired the initial expression of reward-conditioned responses, but their relative contribution to SPN dynamics and behavioral performance diminished with training 43. In a complementary study, Owen and colleagues showed that PV and cholinergic interneurons have dissociable roles during movement: PV cells facilitate movement execution by refining the activation of SPN networks, while CINs synchronize SPN activity to signal the termination of a movement bout 44. Together, these results point to a potential division of labor: SOM interneurons are disproportionately important for gating plasticity and shaping representations during early, flexible, goal-directed learning (especially in dorsomedial striatum), whereas PV interneurons are more important for sharpening performance-related output (especially in dorsolateral striatum), with both subtypes operating alongside–and in some cases regulated by–the cholinergic and dopaminergic signals described above.

The composite picture is therefore considerably more complex than "dopamine is the teacher, acetylcholine sets the learning window." A more accurate summary is that corticostriatal plasticity is governed by a multi-layered neuromodulatory and interneuronal gating architecture in which: (i) cholinergic pauses define the temporal window within which dopamine can drive plasticity, (ii) the phase relationship between acetylcholine and dopamine transients determines whether a given dopamine event functions as a teaching signal or a vigor signal, (iii) muscarinic receptor signaling biases the plasticity landscape toward depression or potentiation, (iv) cholinergic dynamics carry their own error-like signals that are especially important for extinction and behavioral flexibility, (v) CIN activity recruits parallel serotonergic plasticity pathways through nicotinic activation of raphe-striatal axons, and (vi) GABAergic SOM and PV interneurons provide regionally specialized control over SPN excitability, representational selection, and dopamine release that is itself plastic and learning-dependent. The dopaminergic teaching signal, in other words, does not arrive at a passive synaptic substrate; it arrives at a dynamically configured local circuit whose cholinergic, serotonergic, and GABAergic components collectively determine where, when, and in what effective sign the error is allowed to modify the striatal policy.
